Casanova’s attack on Voltaire carries subtext: his effort to secure approval in Venice suggests strategic conformity beneath his apparent religious conviction, especially since freethinking was his most unforgivable offense. His increasingly humble appeals likewise leave room for tension between genuine remorse and desperation. These implications feel natural rather than forced, enriching the portrait of an aging adventurer and a Venetian society in which intellectual obedience matters more than personal misconduct.
